characters: Kofi: a thirteen-year-old Ghanaian JHS 2 sprinter in a green sports vest, lean and observant.
Esi: his fourteen-year-old classmate and 400-metre runner, confident and scientifically sharp.
Ibrahim: Kofi’s relay teammate and close friend, principled and calm.
Baffour: a taller sixteen-year-old JHS 3 student holding an unlabelled dark plastic bottle.
Madam Mensah: the school Guidance and Counselling Coordinator and Social Studies teacher.

narrationPlan.voice: Relatable teen voices for Kofi, Esi, and Ibrahim; pressured older-boy voice for Baffour; calm guidance voice for Madam Mensah
narrationPlan.pace: Steady, relatable, and resolute (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with distinct, natural voices for each JHS student, teacher, and community specialist.
Pause for two seconds at each comprehension check so learners can reason before answering.
Never rush the final page: let the scientific and moral synthesis settle clearly.

music: Rhythmic heartbeat percussion with warm acoustic guitar notes, building quietly to an uplifting finish (placeholder)
culturalNotes: NaCCA CCP Alignment: Integrated Science (B8.3.1.1 / B9.3.1.1 & B8.5.2.1: Human body systems, cellular respiration, and dangers of drug/substance abuse), Social Studies (B7.2.1.1 / B8.2.1.1: Strand 2, Sub-strand 1: Adolescent Reproductive Health, puberty, body image, and peer pressure), and RME (B8.5.1.1 / B9.5.1.1: Strand 5: Ethics & Moral Life—moral decision-making, self-control, and substance abuse prevention).
FDA Ghana & GES SHEP Relevance: Addresses high-caffeine drinks and the risks of unknown or unprescribed medicines; the story does not identify the unknown tablet as tramadol.
Safety Guardrail: The text deliberately gives no quantities or preparation detail for the mixture; do not add any when localising.
Science note: a 200-metre sprint relies heavily on anaerobic respiration, so the story says cells release the most energy with oxygen, not only with oxygen.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated JHS age band (Basic 7 to Basic 9) and BECE conceptual level?
Is anything here scientifically inaccurate, stereotyped, or unsafe for adolescents?
Confirm physiological accuracy distinguishing aerobic respiration from CNS opioid analgesia and stimulant tachycardia.
Ensure puberty timing differences are framed positively to reassure early and late maturers alike.

teacherGuide.overview: Equips JHS students to resist substance abuse and peer pressure by combining accurate human biology, puberty reassurance, practical refusal language, and interfaith moral ethics.
learningGoals: Contrast genuine cellular energy release (respiration) with stimulant and opioid effects on the heart and brain.
Explain why adolescent growth spurts occur on varied biological schedules.
Practise the three-step assertive refusal technique.
Relate Christian, Islamic, and traditional Ghanaian teachings on self-control to real adolescent choices.

beforeReading: Ask: An energy drink contains sugar and caffeine. Which of the two can muscles actually use in respiration, and what does the other one do?
whileReading: Pause on Page 5 and examine why Kofi stays calm rather than arguing with Baffour.
afterReading: Role-play assertive refusal in pairs for sports boosters, exam leakage, and unsafe outings.
discussion: Why are pain signals essential for protecting muscles and organs during sport?
reflection: Which personal goal or family value helps you stand firm against crowd pressure?

mathsExtension.task: Kofi’s resting pulse is 72 bpm. A gentle warm-up raises it by 50%. Find his warm-up heart rate. A student who misused a stimulant recorded a pulse 150% above the same resting value while sitting still. Find that heart rate and explain why it is alarming at rest.
mathsExtension.answer: 108 bpm (warm-up). 180 bpm while sitting still. A pulse of 180 bpm while sitting still is an urgent warning sign requiring prompt medical assessment; exercise heart rates vary by age and individual.

support: Provide printed refusal sentence starters for pair practice.
stretch: Research FDA Ghana regulations on prescription analgesics and caffeine labelling.

factCheck.claim: Caffeine and unprescribed painkillers do not provide cellular energy, and combining them masks physiological warning signals.
factCheck.explanation: Cells derive metabolic energy from glucose via cellular respiration. Stimulants only block adenosine receptors to mask fatigue, while analgesics blunt nociceptive pain signals, risking severe tissue damage.
factCheck.reference: NaCCA CCP Integrated Science B8.3.1.1 / B9.3.1.1 & FDA Ghana public health advisories.
